Not every man knows what he shall sing at the end, Watching the pier as the ship sails away, or what it will seem like When he’s held by the sea’s roar, motionless, there at the end, Or what he shall hope for once it is clear that he’ll never go back. When the time has passed to prune the rose or caress the cat, When the sunset torching the lawn and the full moon icing it down No longer appear, not every man knows what he’ll discover instead. When the weight of the past leans against nothing, and the sky Is no more than remembered light, and the stories of cirrus And cumulus come to a close, and all the birds are suspended in flight, Not every man knows what is waiting for him, or what he shall sing When the ship he is on slips into darkness, there at the end.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Not, Watching, When

outputs.L1:
Not every man knows what he will sing at the end,  
watching the pier as the ship sails away, or what it will be like  
when he is held motionless by the sea’s roar, there at the end,  
or what he will hope for once it is clear he will never return.  

When the time has passed to prune the rose or caress the cat,  
when the sunset, torching the lawn, and the full moon, icing it down,  
no longer appear, not every man knows what he will discover instead.  

When the weight of the past leans against nothing, and the sky  
is no more than remembered light, and the stories of cirrus  
and cumulus come to a close, and all the birds hang suspended in flight,  
not every man knows what is waiting for him, or what he will sing  
when the ship he is on slips into darkness, there at the end.
outputs.L2:
No man can be certain what song will come to him in the final moment,  
as he looks back toward the pier while the vessel moves out to sea;  
nor can he know how it will feel  
to stand still at the edge, enclosed by the ocean’s thunder,  
or what he will long for once he understands there is no return.

After the season for trimming roses has gone by,  
after there is no more time to stroke the cat,  
after the evening sun no longer sets the grass ablaze  
and the round moon no longer cools it with pale light,  
not every man can tell what will appear in their place.

When the burden of memory rests on emptiness,  
when the sky is only brightness recalled,  
when the tales told by cirrus and cumulus clouds have ended,  
and every bird hangs fixed in the air,  
not every man knows what awaits him,  
or what song he will raise  
as the ship carrying him glides into the dark,  
there, at the very end.
outputs.L3:
The poem reflects on the uncertainty people face at the end of life. It considers the moment when a person reaches a point from which there is no return, and it emphasizes how little anyone can truly know about what that experience will be like. We may imagine our final thoughts or feelings, but the poem suggests that such certainty is impossible. No one can fully predict what they will feel, what they will hope for, or what they will understand when the familiar world begins to fall away.

As the end approaches, the ordinary pleasures and routines of earthly life lose their presence. The things that once gave shape and meaning to daily existence—simple comforts, familiar habits, conversations, and the visible details of the world—begin to recede. What once seemed vivid and important becomes distant. The poem presents this movement as a gradual fading, where life’s usual attachments no longer hold the same force.

Memories and stories also begin to disappear into stillness. The images through which a person has understood the world—places, people, voices, and experiences—grow dim. Instead of offering clear meaning or reassurance, they seem to dissolve into silence and darkness. This fading creates a solemn atmosphere, suggesting that death is not only the end of physical life but also a departure from the known patterns of memory and perception.

The final image of a ship slipping into darkness powerfully represents this mysterious passage toward death. A ship leaving sight suggests movement into an unknown realm, beyond the reach of those who remain behind. It does not provide a clear answer about what comes next; instead, it captures the uncertainty and mystery of the final journey. Through this image, the poem presents death as a quiet departure into darkness, where human knowledge and earthly experience can no longer follow.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents death as a final departure into uncertainty, using the image of a ship leaving shore to suggest a journey from the known world into an unknown destination. Like a vessel slowly disappearing beyond the horizon, the dying person moves away from the sight and reach of those left behind. This image creates a sense of quiet separation rather than sudden violence: death is imagined as a gradual fading, a movement out of familiar view. The shore represents the world of human relationships, memories, and daily life, while the open sea suggests mystery, distance, and the limits of human understanding.

Natural images of fading light, dimming landscapes, or vanishing scenes deepen this sense of departure. The world that once seemed solid and familiar begins to dissolve, as if earthly attachments lose their shape at the moment of death. Places, voices, and relationships that gave life meaning are left behind, and the speaker is forced to confront the painful absence created by this separation. These images emphasize not only the experience of the one who departs, but also the grief of those who remain, watching as someone they love passes beyond their reach.

At the same time, the poem does not claim to know what lies beyond death. Instead, it acknowledges the limits of human knowledge. No one can fully describe what waits at the end of life, because death takes each person beyond the boundaries of ordinary experience. This uncertainty gives the poem its emotional and philosophical power. Mortality is not presented simply as an ending, but as a profound mystery shaped by memory, loss, absence, and the unknown.

Ultimately, the poem reflects on the human desire to understand death while recognizing that such understanding may never be complete. The departing ship, the fading natural world, and the loss of familiar earthly ties all point toward the same truth: death removes a person from the visible world, but it does not answer the questions left behind. What remains is a mixture of sorrow, wonder, and uncertainty, as the living continue to remember those who have gone while imagining a destination they cannot see.
outputs.L5:
**Not Watching When It Matters**

Sometimes, the most important moments happen when we are not watching. A child takes their first brave step when no one is holding the camera. A flower opens quietly in the early morning. A friend hides their sadness behind a smile while everyone is too busy to notice.

We often think that watching means understanding, but that is not always true. We may look at something and still fail to see its meaning. When we are distracted, tired, or careless, life continues around us without waiting for our attention.

That is why it is important to be present. Not every moment can be repeated, and not every feeling can be explained later. When we truly pay attention, we notice more than actions—we notice emotions, silence, and change.

Being there does not always mean watching with our eyes. Sometimes it means listening, caring, and understanding when someone needs us most.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic free-verse poem about a man facing death, using imagery of a ship leaving a pier, the sea, sunset, moonlight, birds, clouds, and the unknown final song.
counterfactuals.output:
At the end, he stands like a pier  
that has forgotten the weight of footsteps,  
hands resting on the rail  
as if wood could answer back.

The ship waits below him,  
black hull breathing against the tide,  
ropes slackening one by one  
like old promises released from the mouth.

Behind him, the town grows quiet—  
windows dim, doors closing softly,  
the small lamps of a life  
lowered into evening.

Ahead, the sea opens,  
dark and without explanation.  
It does not threaten.  
It does not welcome.  
It simply moves,  
vast as a thought he can no longer finish.

Sunset spills its last gold  
across the water,  
a tired fire folding itself  
into the blue bruise of distance.

Above, clouds drift like unsent letters,  
their edges torn by wind.  
Birds wheel once over the pier,  
crying out in voices  
that sound almost like names,  
then vanish toward the reddening west.

He listens.

Somewhere beyond the harbor,  
beyond the bell,  
beyond the gulls and their salt-white wings,  
there is said to be a final song—  
not learned, not remembered,  
not sung by any living throat.

Moonlight rises quietly  
to silver the deck,  
to soften the ropes,  
to lay a pale hand  
upon his shoulder.

The ship begins to leave.

No thunder,  
no command,  
only the slow surrender  
of wood from shore,  
the widening strip of water  
between what loved him  
and what waits.

He does not wave.  
He watches the pier grow small,  
its posts dark fingers  
reaching into the tide.

The birds are gone now.  
The clouds close over the sun.  
The sea takes the moon  
and breaks it into trembling pieces.

And he, at last,  
turns toward the horizon—  
toward that vast, uncharted hush,  
where every voyage ends  
in the unknown final song.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary poem in the style of modern American elegiac verse, beginning with the idea that not every man knows what he will sing at the end.
counterfactuals.output:
Not every man knows what he will sing at the end.  
Some carry only a little weather in the mouth,  
a porch-light trembling over the last field,  
the smell of rain lifting from blacktop  
after a long refusal.

Some have rehearsed the names of the dead  
until the names become a room  
they can enter without knocking.  
Some forget even their own faces  
and reach, instead, for a cup of water,  
for the sleeve of a daughter,  
for the old dog’s weight at the foot of the bed.

What is a life, then, but the tuning  
of an instrument no one sees?  
All day the world leans close—  
the freight train dragging its iron hymn  
through the outskirts,  
the cottonwoods loosening their pale coins  
into the ditch,  
the hospital window filling with afternoon  
as if light itself could be forgiven.

I used to think the last song  
would have grandeur:  
a door thrown open,  
a choir of birds rising from the elm,  
some bright country of the spirit  
answering from beyond the hills.

But now I think it may be smaller—  
the sound of a match struck in a dark kitchen,  
a mother calling a child in from snow,  
the creek speaking under its ice  
in the language of going on.

And if the voice fails,  
if the throat closes like a flower at dusk,  
perhaps the song continues elsewhere:  
in the dust motes turning above the bed,  
in the hands that wash the body,  
in the shovel’s clean bite,  
in the grass returning without bitterness  
over everything we were.

Not every man knows what he will sing.  
He may arrive empty-handed,  
astonished to find the music waiting—  
not in him, but around him:  
the wind in the eaves,  
the far-off bells of traffic,  
the small, persistent mercy  
of the world  
still asking to be heard.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a reflective poem about mortality and departure, where the speaker imagines someone on a ship sailing into darkness and wondering what remains when he can never return.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk I saw him board the quiet ship,  
its lanterns trembling like last words in rain.  
The harbor held its breath around the slip,  
and ropes fell loose from all he knew by name.  

He did not wave for long. The dark came down  
and folded mast and sail into its hand;  
the water took the moonlight from the town,  
the tide erased his footprints from the sand.  

I wondered then what stays when one is gone—  
the chair still turned a little toward the fire,  
a coat that keeps the shape of being worn,  
a song half-lifted from a broken lyre.  

Does love remain, or only love’s outline,  
a warmth the cooling rooms cannot explain?  
Do voices sink beneath the closing brine,  
or rise in us whenever we speak again?  

He sailed where no returning sail is seen,  
past chart and bell, past harbor-light and foam;  
yet in the dark between what is and has been,  
we keep his absence like a second home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-stanza, lyrical meditation on the end of life, incorporating roses, a cat, lawn at sunset, a full moon, remembered sky, cirrus and cumulus clouds, and suspended birds.
counterfactuals.output: At the end, perhaps, it will be gentle: roses loosening their red breath by the gate, the cat a quiet shadow crossing the lawn at sunset, each blade holding a last gold fire; above, the full moon will rise like a thought I almost understand, and the remembered sky will gather me back—its cirrus veils, its cumulus islands, its blue rooms of childhood and rain—while suspended birds hang for one trembling instant between flight and farewell, as if the world itself has paused to listen, as if dying were only this: the heart unclasping, petal by petal, into the luminous dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a somber poem with long flowing lines about the uncertainty of death, using repeated phrasing like “Not every man knows” and ending with a ship slipping into darkness.
counterfactuals.output:
Not every man knows when the last bell begins its trembling in the ribs,  
or whether the hour comes softly, like rain finding the roof at midnight,  
or with the sudden iron cry of a gate thrown open in a storm.  

Not every man knows the shape of the road that will carry him away,  
whether it bends through a field of remembered sunlight,  
or narrows beneath black branches where no familiar voice can follow.  

Not every man knows what waits beyond the closing of the eyes,  
whether silence is a room, or a sea, or only the breath held forever,  
while the living stand with their hands full of flowers and unanswered names.  

Not every man knows if he has loved enough to be forgiven by the earth,  
if his small fires warmed anyone through winter,  
if the words he left behind will rise like smoke or sink like stones.  

Not every man knows the date written in dust beside his door,  
nor hears the footfall approaching through the years, patient and unhurried,  
nor sees how the evening gathers itself around his shoulders.  

Not every man knows, and so he walks beneath the dimming sky,  
counting stars as if they were promises, touching the faces of those he loves,  
while far off, beyond the harbor lights, a ship slips into darkness.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
